extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and inventors drafting U.S. software patent claims after Alice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidance for preparing software-related patent claims and specification language to survive Alice §101 analysis and related rejections in the U.S. Focuses on tying claims to technical improvements, specificity, hardware embodiments, and parallel claim sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step eligibility discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to an abstract idea? Step 2: Does the claim recite an 'inventive concept' that amounts to significantly more?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot avoid Step 1 by clever drafting. You can win Step 2 by tying the claim to a specific technical improvement. Treat the Alice two-step as a drafting discipline rather than an unpredictable doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor the claim in a technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening of your specification should describe a technical problem in the operation of a computer (latency, memory footprint, packet loss, indexing inefficiency, security vulnerability). Not a business problem. Not 'users find it hard to...'. A computer problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly frame the invention as solving technical/computer-operational issues. Use concrete problems (e.g., latency, memory footprint) rather than user/business-facing descriptions to support §101 arguments and examiner citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite specific technical steps, not outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recite concrete steps and mechanisms rather than high-level outcomes (e.g., avoid 'determining a recommendation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed technical phrasing: e.g., 'applying a hashed Bloom filter to the user-interaction log to identify candidate items, then ranking the candidates using a learned weight matrix stored in GPU memory.' Specificity increases chances of eligibility and distinguishes from abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure result-oriented language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid claiming only the result (e.g., 'A method for predicting customer churn' is suspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer phrasing that recites how the result is achieved: e.g., 'A method for predicting customer churn comprising training a gradient-boosted decision tree on a feature set including session timing residuals...' The closer the claim stays to the result only, the closer it is to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a hardware-tied embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the invention is fundamentally algorithmic, include at least one claim that recites concrete hardware: a specific sensor, a specific accelerator, a particular memory architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a machine-tied claim to invoke the 'machine prong' rhetorically (historic Bilski test). Concrete hardware elements can help resist §101 rejections and show claimed subject matter affects machine functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the §101 argument into the specification (Technical Improvements paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the detailed description, include a paragraph titled 'Technical Improvements' that explicitly catalogs how the claimed system improves the functioning of a computer (e.g., 'reduces query latency by 40%,' 'eliminates the need for a roundtrip to the database server').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and judges quote these paragraphs. Explicitly state measurable/technical improvements to support Step 2 inventive-concept arguments and to make it easier for examiners/judges to find technical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: File parallel claim sets (method, apparatus, CRM)
rubrics_metrics.description: File parallel claim sets: method, system/apparatus, and computer-readable medium (CRM) claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different defendants infringe different claim types and different judges prefer different formats. Having multiple claim types increases enforcement and examination robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'black box' claims; disclose sufficient architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites 'a model trained to...' without describing the architecture invites both §101 (abstract idea) and §112 (enablement) rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite enough of the model architecture and implementation detail that a skilled person could implement it. Provide architecture, training procedure, storage details, and hardware context to reduce risk of 101/112 rejections.
